say: You give it a **type of data** and a question. It gives back the graph or number that answers the question, and a reason.

The key idea: match the tool to the data. Numbers that can have a few extreme values need the **median**; two numerical measures on the same people need a scatter plot; shares of a whole need a pie chart.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level asked for it on Paper 2 in 2017 (Question 9(b)(iii)) and 2018 (Question 7(b)), as a short part: pick the best option, or say whether a mean can be trusted, and give a reason.

example.question: Six students are asked how much pocket money they get each week (in euro): $5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 40$. Which average describes a typical student better, the mean or the median? Calculate both and give a reason.

steps.title: Spot the odd value
steps.say: Look at the data first. One value, $\hl{1}{40}$, is far bigger than the rest. An extreme value drags the mean up but hardly moves the median.

lines.text: Five students get $8$ or less. One gets $40$.

steps.title: Calculate the mean
steps.say: Add the values and divide by how many there are.

steps.title: Calculate the median
steps.say: The data is already in order. With six values, the median is halfway between the 3rd and 4th.

steps.title: Choose and explain
steps.say: The mean of $12$ is bigger than what five of the six students get. The median is not pulled by the $40$.

lines.text: Use the **median**: the $40$ is extreme, so the mean is not typical.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{Median} = 6.5\text{, because the extreme value } 40 \text{ pulls the mean up to } 12

ordinary.tip: Name your choice and give a reason that uses the data. A reason with no choice named earns nothing.

sources.quote: A reason with no year identified.

ordinary.tip: When the question is open, several answers can be right. Pick one and justify it with the numbers.
A mean worked out from percentages, ignoring the group sizes, is unreliable. Say so when asked about it.

say: You give it a histogram or stem-and-leaf plot, or the data behind one. It says whether the shape is **symmetric**, or has a long tail to one side (**skew**).
The key idea: the tail pulls the mean toward it. A long right tail is positive skew, with mean above median. A long left tail is negative skew, with mean below median.

example.question: The number of text messages sent by eight students in one day is: $1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 24$. Find the mean and the median. What does this tell you about the shape of the distribution?

steps.title: Find the mean
steps.say: Add all the values and divide by $8$.

steps.title: Find the median
steps.say: The data is in order. With eight values, the median is halfway between the 4th and 5th.

steps.title: Compare them
steps.say: Subtract. A positive difference means the mean sits above the median.

steps.title: Name the shape
steps.say: The mean is above the median. The single big value $24$ is a long tail on the right, and it pulls the mean up.

lines.text: Mean $>$ median, so the distribution is **positively skewed**.

say: You give it two data sets. It puts them on one **back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot**, then compares their centre and spread.
The key idea: both sets share one column of stems. The leaves of one grow to the left, the other to the right, so the two shapes sit side by side.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level asked for it on Paper 2 in 2015, 2016, 2022 and 2024, in parts worth 5 to 15 marks: complete the plot, find centre and spread, then write a conclusion.

example.question: The times, in seconds, that seven students took to finish a puzzle in two weeks are: Week 1: $28, 35, 21, 47, 33, 24, 42$. Week 2: $36, 22, 31, 18, 38, 29, 23$. Show the data on a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot and compare the two weeks using the median and the range.

steps.title: Draw the plot
steps.say: Use the tens as stems. Put Week 1 leaves on the right and Week 2 leaves on the left, each row in order, smallest next to the stem.

lines.text: Key: $2 | 3 | 5$ means $32$ seconds in Week 2 and $35$ in Week 1.

steps.title: Find the medians
steps.say: With seven values, the median is the 4th one in order. Read it off the plot.

steps.title: Find the ranges
steps.say: The range is the biggest value minus the smallest.

steps.title: Write the conclusion
steps.say: Say what each number shows, in words, about both weeks.

lines.text: Week 2 is quicker: its median is $4$ seconds lower.
Week 2 is more consistent: its range is $20$, against $26$.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{Week 2 was faster (median } 29 < 33\text{) and less spread out (range } 20 < 26\text{)}

ordinary.tip: Get every value onto the plot first. Leaves out of order are still accepted.

sources.quote: Accept values that are not in order

ordinary.tip: If you cannot finish the plot, sort the data. Effort at ordering earns partial credit.
Write the formula with the numbers put in before you calculate. That earns high partial credit.
A conclusion must say in words what changed, such as increase. A number alone is not enough.

say: You give it a research question. It gives back a **plan** for collecting the data and survey questions that do not push people toward an answer.
The key idea: every group you care about must get a fair share of the sample, and a question must not hint at the answer you hope for.

example.question: A school of $800$ students has four year groups of $200$. The principal wants to find out what students think of the canteen, and plans to ask: "Don't you agree the canteen food is awful?" She will survey $40$ students. Rewrite the question fairly and say how many students to ask from each year group.

steps.title: Spot the bias
steps.say: A question is **leading** if it hints at the answer. The words "Don't you agree" and "awful" push students toward one reply.

lines.text: The question pushes the student to say yes.

steps.title: Reword it fairly
steps.say: Take out the hint. Ask for an opinion and offer balanced choices.

lines.text: "How would you rate the canteen food?" Very good, good, average, poor, very poor.

steps.title: Find the sampling fraction
steps.say: Each year group should be represented in proportion. $40$ out of $800$ is the fraction of students to ask.

steps.title: Students from each year
steps.say: Each year group has $200$ students. Take that fraction of each, and choose them at random within the year.

lines.text: Ask $10$ students from each of the four year groups.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: \text{Ask } 10 \text{ from each year group, using a neutral question}
